summary:
Latvia has no procedure for legal gender recognition. Transgender and nonbinary Latvians cannot obtain a corrected gender marker, and no targeted legislation has been adopted; coalition members of parliament said in June 2025 that trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." One trans immigrant interviewed by LSM stated that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been in force since 1 July 2024. They do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, and no legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities is documented in the sources.

The most significant institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14. A 2020 attack on a gay couple in Riga was not prosecuted as a hate crime even though the aggressor admitted using anti-gay slurs; the matter was reduced to a minor public-order offence carrying a lenient fine. The Court held that the failure to prosecute inhuman treatment and the discriminatory handling of the case violated the prohibition of inhuman treatment, the right to private life and the non-discrimination guarantee, and the Strasbourg Observers analysis of the judgment notes that states must investigate and punish hate-motivated attacks thoroughly as a positive obligation.

Enforcement failures are documented beyond that case. In Daugavpils, two people were attacked and police closed the matter until the Prosecutor General ordered the investigation reopened. Following the ECtHR ruling, the Prosecutor General also reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. Former MEP Tatjana Mamikins faced an investigation over homophobic posts and left for Russia.

Protection machinery does function in some channels. In 2025 an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI applicant.

Public hostility remains visible from senior religious figures: in 2007 Cardinal Jānis Pujats of Riga described homosexuality as "total corruption in the sexual arena" and demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and large counter-demonstrations against Pride.
